metrics.label: Heart rate
metrics.device: Finger pulse oximeter or chest strap
how: Rest, seated or restrained, for 5 minutes. No exercise in the last 30 minutes.
Clip the pulse oximeter on a warm fingertip, or wear the chest strap.
Keep still for 30 seconds and read the beats per minute.
metrics.why: Resting heart rate is a quick window into the cardiovascular system. Fever, dehydration, stress, poor sleep and heart deconditioning all push it up.
metrics.space: In weightlessness the heart works less and can decondition. Fluid shift and stress change its rhythm, and returning to gravity can make it race.

guide.ok: Within your normal range. Keep your exercise routine going.
guide.watch: Slightly out of range. Rest for 10 minutes, drink water and measure again. If it stays out of range, log how you feel and re-check in 4 hours.
guide.act: Out of the safe range. Stop strenuous activity and measure again now. If confirmed, call the Crew Medical Officer. With chest pain, fainting or breathlessness, open EMERGENCY.

metrics.escalate: Call the Crew Medical Officer if resting heart rate stays below 40 or above 120, or with palpitations, chest pain or fainting.

metrics.label: Blood pressure
how: Sit or strap in with your feet supported and rest for 5 minutes.
Wrap the cuff on your bare upper arm, 2 cm above the elbow, at heart level.
Stay silent and still while it inflates. Record systolic / diastolic.
metrics.why: Blood pressure shows how hard the heart and vessels are working. It reveals cardiovascular strain early and helps prepare the body for gravity on landing.
metrics.space: Without gravity, about 2 litres of fluid shift toward the head. The body re-tunes blood pressure control, which can lead to dizziness or fainting when gravity returns.

guide.watch: Borderline. Rest quietly for 15 minutes and measure again. Go easy on salt and caffeine today and re-check tonight.
guide.act: Out of range. Measure again on the other arm. If it is still 140/90 or higher, or the top number is below 85, notify the Crew Medical Officer. With headache, vision change or chest pain, open EMERGENCY.

metrics.escalate: Call the Crew Medical Officer for repeated readings of 140/90 or higher, systolic below 85, or symptoms such as headache, dizziness or vision change.

metrics.label: Blood oxygen
how: Warm your hand and remove anything covering the fingertip.
Clip the oximeter on and keep the hand still at heart level.
Wait 30 seconds for a stable reading.
metrics.why: Oxygen saturation shows whether your lungs, blood and the cabin air are doing their job.
metrics.space: A sealed cabin can build up CO2. Lunar and Martian dust can irritate the airways, and a chest infection spreads easily in a small crew.

guide.watch: A bit low. Measure on another finger and check the cabin CO2 / O2 display. Take slow, deep breaths and re-check in 10 minutes.
guide.act: Low oxygen. Measure again now. If confirmed, call the Crew Medical Officer and check the cabin atmosphere. With breathlessness or confusion, open EMERGENCY.

metrics.escalate: Call the Crew Medical Officer if SpO2 stays below 92%, and immediately if below 90% or with breathlessness.

metrics.label: Breathing rate
how: Sit still for 2 minutes.
Count breaths for 30 seconds: one rise and fall is one breath. A crewmate can count quietly.
Multiply by 2.
metrics.why: Breathing rate rises early with infection, fever, high CO2, anxiety or heart strain, often before anything else changes.
metrics.space: CO2 pockets can form where air does not circulate, such as around a sleeping bag. Fast breathing can be the body's first response.

guide.watch: Re-count after 5 minutes of calm breathing. Check temperature and SpO2 as well.
guide.act: Call the Crew Medical Officer and check the cabin CO2. With breathlessness or chest pain, open EMERGENCY.

metrics.escalate: Call the Crew Medical Officer if breathing stays above 24 per minute at rest.

metrics.label: Body temperature
how: No eating, drinking or exercise for 15 minutes before measuring.
Place the thermometer under the tongue, or use the forehead sensor.
Wait for the beep and record °C.
metrics.why: Fever is the body's first infection alarm. In a closed habitat, catching an infection early protects the whole crew.
metrics.space: Immune function changes in space, and dormant viruses can reactivate. Crew core temperature can also run up to about 1 °C higher on long missions, so ASTRA also flags a reading that is unusual for you, even inside the normal range.

guide.watch: Slightly off. Drink fluids, rest and re-check in 2 hours. Note any chills, cough or sore throat.
guide.act: Fever above 38 °C (or below 35.5 °C). Notify the Crew Medical Officer, limit close contact with crewmates and log symptoms every 2 hours.

metrics.escalate: Call the Crew Medical Officer for any fever above 38 °C, and immediately above 39.5 °C.

metrics.label: Blood glucose
how: Measure fasting, before breakfast.
Clean the fingertip and lance its side. In weightlessness the blood forms a dome and won't drip.
Touch the strip to the drop and read mg/dL.
metrics.why: Glucose shows how the body turns food into energy and links nutrition, activity and metabolism.
metrics.space: Spaceflight can reduce insulin sensitivity, and long missions have a fixed, limited menu. Lower activity makes it worse.

guide.watch: Outside the fasting target. If low (below 70): eat 15 g of fast carbohydrate and re-test in 15 minutes. If high: re-test tomorrow fasting and review meals and activity.
guide.act: Out of range. Below 55: take fast carbohydrate now, re-test in 15 minutes and tell a crewmate. 126 or higher fasting: re-test and notify the Crew Medical Officer.

metrics.escalate: Call the Crew Medical Officer for fasting values of 126 or higher on two days, or any value below 55.

metrics.label: Fluid intake
metrics.device: Drink bag counter / water dispenser log
how: Add up the drink bags and water you have had today.
Include water used to rehydrate food.
Enter the total in litres.
metrics.why: Fluids keep blood volume and the kidneys healthy and help you think clearly.
metrics.space: You feel less thirsty in weightlessness. Calcium released from shrinking bones raises the risk of kidney stones, and plenty of water lowers it.

guide.watch: A bit low. Drink 500 ml over the next hour and set a reminder.
guide.act: Too low (or too high). Drink steadily to reach at least 2 L, and tell the Crew Medical Officer if you have flank pain or dark urine.

metrics.escalate: Call the Crew Medical Officer for flank or back pain with low intake. It can be a kidney stone.
prevent: Keep a drink bag in sight

metrics.label: Body mass
how: Measure before breakfast, after using the toilet.
Strap into the mass device and hold still while it oscillates. Scales don't work in weightlessness.
Read the mass in kg.
metrics.why: Weight loss is an early sign that you are not eating enough or are losing muscle.
metrics.space: Appetite often drops in space, and muscle shrinks without gravity. Many crews lose weight without noticing.

guide.ok: Within 3% of your mission reference mass.
guide.watch: 3-5% change from your reference. Eat the full menu, add snacks, and keep resistive exercise.
guide.act: More than 5% change. Tell the Crew Medical Officer and review your diet plan with ground nutrition.

metrics.escalate: Call the Crew Medical Officer for a change of more than 5% from your reference mass.

metrics.label: Food intake
how: Look at today's meal plan.
Estimate how much of it you ate, as a percentage: the full plan is 100%.
Count snacks and drinks that have calories.
metrics.why: Eating enough protects muscle, bone, immunity and mood. Under-eating is common on long missions and slowly weakens every other system.
metrics.space: Appetite drops in weightlessness, food gets monotonous and some vitamins degrade over months, so crews often eat only about 80% of what they need. Calcium and vitamin D matter more while bones are losing mass.

guide.watch: Below plan. Add a snack with protein, try a different menu item or share a crew meal.
guide.act: Well below plan (or far above it). Tell the Crew Medical Officer, especially with weight loss, nausea or low mood.

metrics.escalate: Call the Crew Medical Officer if you eat less than 75% of plan for 3 days, or with weight loss above 3%.
prevent: Calcium and vitamin D as prescribed

metrics.label: Sleep
how: Read last night's hours from your sleep watch, or estimate from lights-out to wake-up.
Subtract time spent awake during the night.
Note what disturbed you: noise, light, temperature or worries.
metrics.why: Sleep debt quietly erodes mood, reaction time and safety, and you often don't notice it yourself.
metrics.space: Noise, workload, odd light cycles (16 sunrises a day in orbit) and isolation shorten crew sleep. Many astronauts average under 6.5 hours.

guide.ok: Good night. Keep the same sleep window.
guide.watch: Short night. Protect tonight's 8.5-hour window, dim screens an hour before bed and avoid caffeine after 14:00.
guide.act: Serious sleep debt. Tell the Commander before any critical task, schedule recovery sleep and talk to the Crew Medical Officer about sleep support.

metrics.escalate: Tell the Crew Medical Officer if sleep is under 6 hours on 3 nights in a row.

metrics.label: Mood
how: Pause for 30 seconds and notice how you feel right now.
Pick the face that fits best. There is no wrong answer.
Your answer stays private unless you choose to share it.
metrics.why: Low mood is easier to fix early, and it protects the whole crew's cohesion.
metrics.space: Isolation, confinement, monotony and distance from loved ones are major spaceflight hazards on long missions.

guide.ok: Good. Keep the routines that help you.
guide.watch: A bit low. Plan something you enjoy, call family at the next comm window, and get some exercise and light.
guide.act: Low mood. You're not alone. Talk to a trusted crewmate or the Crew Medical Officer today, and book a private session with ground psychological support.

metrics.escalate: Talk to the Crew Medical Officer if mood stays at 2 or lower, or 3 for a week.

metrics.label: Reaction time
how: Sit comfortably with your finger ready.
Tap the pad the moment it turns green. There are 3 trials.
Your score is the average.
metrics.why: A one-minute alertness test. Fatigue, sleep debt, stress and high CO2 slow you down before you notice. It matters before EVAs, docking or driving a rover.
metrics.space: Sleep loss, workload and radiation exposure can all affect attention and reaction speed.

guide.ok: Sharp. Good to go for critical tasks.
guide.watch: Slower than usual. Avoid critical tasks for now, rest, drink water and re-test in 2 hours.
guide.act: Much slower. Do not perform critical operations. Tell the Commander and re-test after sleep.

metrics.escalate: Tell the Commander before any critical task if reaction time is above 400 ms.

metrics.label: Exercise
how: Do resistive loading (squats, deadlifts, heel raises) plus aerobic work (treadmill or cycle).
Count the warm-up but not the breaks.
Enter today's total minutes.
metrics.why: Loading bones and muscles every day is the main defence against bone loss and deconditioning.
metrics.space: Unloaded bones lose roughly 1-1.5% of their mass per month, most at the hips and spine. Space-station crews exercise about 2 hours a day to slow this.

guide.ok: Target met. Your bones and muscles thank you.
guide.watch: Below the 2-hour target. Add a resistive session today that loads the legs, hips and spine.
guide.act: Far below target. Tell the Commander. Rescheduling exercise is a mission priority, not an option.

metrics.escalate: Tell the Commander if exercise falls below 60 minutes on 2 days in a row.
prevent: Book exercise like any other task

metrics.label: Vision check
how: Hold the tablet at reading distance in good light. Wear your usual glasses.
Cover one eye and look only at the centre dot.
Notice whether any lines look wavy, blurred or missing. Then repeat with the other eye.
metrics.why: A simple weekly self-check that catches vision changes early.
metrics.space: Fluid shift toward the head raises pressure behind the eyes. Many long-duration crew members develop Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS): optic-disc swelling, flattening of the eye and blurred near vision.

guide.ok: No distortion. Check again next week.
guide.watch: Slight blur. Re-check tomorrow and mention it to the Crew Medical Officer. The ground team may request an eye ultrasound.
guide.act: Lines look wavy or missing. Tell the Crew Medical Officer today. An onboard eye examination is needed.

metrics.escalate: Tell the Crew Medical Officer about any new blur, wavy or missing lines.

metrics.label: Symptom check
how: Think about the last 24 hours.
Tick every symptom you noticed, even mild ones.
Red-flag symptoms (chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, sudden vision change) mean EMERGENCY.
metrics.why: Small symptoms often appear before measurements change. Patterns across the crew can reveal an infection or an air-quality problem.
metrics.space: Headaches (CO2), congestion (fluid shift), back pain (spine lengthening) and nausea are common in spaceflight.

guide.watch: Some symptoms. Rest, drink water and re-check tomorrow. ASTRA will watch for patterns.
guide.act: Several symptoms, or a red-flag symptom. Tell the Crew Medical Officer now. Red-flag symptoms: open EMERGENCY.

metrics.escalate: Any red-flag symptom means an immediate call to the Crew Medical Officer and EMERGENCY.

organs.name: Brain & behavior
organs.function: Controls mood, sleep, attention, decisions and, with the inner ear, balance: the crew's most important tool.
organs.space: Isolation, confinement, odd light cycles and workload disturb sleep and mood. Deep-space radiation may affect cognition over long missions. The inner ear's balance organs misread weightlessness at first (space motion sickness) and again after landing, when balance takes days to recover.
actions: Call family or psych support at the next comm window

organs.name: Eyes & vision
organs.function: Vision for every task, from reading displays to docking.
organs.space: Fluid shift toward the head can swell the optic disc, where the optic nerve enters the eye, and flatten the eye: Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).
actions: Ground may request an eye ultrasound

organs.name: Heart & circulation
organs.function: Pumps blood and oxygen to every organ.
organs.space: With less work to do the heart can decondition. Fluid shift changes blood pressure, and returning to gravity can cause dizziness or fainting.
actions: Report chest pain or fainting at once

organs.name: Lungs & breathing
organs.function: Brings oxygen in and removes CO2.
organs.space: CO2 can build up in a sealed cabin. On the Moon and Mars, fine reactive dust can irritate the airways after EVAs.
actions: Check cabin CO2 if you have a headache

organs.name: Metabolism & nutrition
organs.function: Turns food into energy and keeps blood sugar stable.
organs.space: Appetite changes, a limited menu and less activity can lead to weight loss and lower insulin sensitivity.

organs.name: Immune system
organs.function: Defends against infection. Fever is its alarm signal.
organs.space: Stress, radiation and closed living change immune function. Dormant viruses can reactivate, and microbes spread easily in a sealed habitat.
actions: Report fever or sore throat early
Keep personal items separate if ill

organs.name: Kidneys & fluids
organs.function: Filter the blood and balance fluids and minerals.
organs.space: Calcium released from shrinking bones raises kidney-stone risk, and the sense of thirst is weaker in weightlessness.
actions: Drink at least 2 L a day

organs.name: Bones & muscles
organs.function: Bones and muscles give support, movement and calcium storage.
organs.space: Unloaded bones lose roughly 1-1.5% of their mass per month, most at the hips and spine. Anti-gravity muscles of the calves, thighs, hips and back waste fastest, and the spine lengthens, causing back pain.
actions: Load the hips, legs and spine

squat.name: Squat
squat.why: Loads the hips and spine, where astronauts lose the most bone: about 1-1.5 % a month without it.
cues: Feet shoulder-width, bar across the upper back
Sit back until thighs are level
Drive up through the heels; breathe out on the way up

deadlift.name: Deadlift
deadlift.why: Keeps the back and hip muscles strong; back pain is common after the spine lengthens in microgravity.
cues: Hinge at the hips, back flat
Bar close to the shins
Stand tall, squeeze the glutes at the top

heel_raise.name: Heel raise
heel_raise.why: Calf muscles shrink fastest in microgravity because feet no longer carry weight.
cues: Bar on the shoulders, knees soft
Rise onto the balls of the feet
Lower slowly, 2 seconds down

press.name: Bench press
press.why: Upper-body strength for EVA suit work, hatch operations and emergency egress.
cues: Shoulder blades pulled back
Lower the bar to mid-chest
Press up and slightly back

row.name: Seated row
row.why: Upper-body pulling strength for suit work and hatch operations; the flywheel loads both directions.
cues: Feet braced, back tall
Pull the handle to the lower ribs
Let the flywheel pull you back slowly

run.name: Treadmill run
run.why: Running is the only aerobic exercise that also gives bones the impact they need.
cues: Harness snug at hips and shoulders
Short, quick steps
Land mid-foot under the hips

cycle_intervals.name: Cycle intervals
cycle_intervals.why: Short hard intervals keep aerobic fitness (VO2max) high in a fraction of the time.
cues: Clip in, hands light on the bars
Hard: above 90 % of max heart rate
Easy pedalling between efforts

cycle_steady.name: Steady ride
cycle_steady.why: Steady endurance work builds the base for EVAs and long work days.
cues: Hold a pace you could talk at
About 70-75 % of max heart rate
Keep cadence smooth, 70-90 rpm

ared.name: ARED
ared.note: Vacuum cylinders give up to about 270 kg (600 lb) of load, like a barbell on Earth.

t2.name: T2 treadmill
t2.note: A harness and bungees pull you onto the belt so your feet take your weight.

cevis.name: CEVIS
cevis.full: Cycle Ergometer with Vibration Isolation and Stabilization
cevis.note: A seatless bike: you clip your shoes in and pedal, held in place by your feet.

flywheel.name: Flywheel
flywheel.note: A shoebox-sized flywheel, as on Orion: a cable resists both the pull and the return.

cycle.name: Cycle ergometer
cycle.note: A small seatless bike that bolts to the floor of the habitat.

weights.name: Free weights
weights.note: In partial gravity you need extra load: your body weighs only a fraction of Earth weight.

treadmill.name: Treadmill
treadmill.note: Partial gravity lets you run without a harness, but impact is lower than on Earth.
